title: WHY WOULD A LOVING GOD SEND ANYONE TO HELL?
paragraphs: WHY WOULD A LOVING GOD SEND ANYONE TO HELL?
The Question That Has Kept Millions Awake at Night
There are questions people ask out loud.
Then there are questions people whisper in the dark.
Questions that emerge when a loved one dies unexpectedly.
Questions that appear when someone reads the Bible and suddenly encounters words they wish were not there.
This is one of those questions.
Why would He send anyone to hell?
For many people, this is not merely a theological issue.
A mother wonders about a son who rejected Christ.
A wife thinks about a husband who never believed.
A believer remembers old friends who mocked the Gospel and died years ago.
An atheist asks it as an objection.
A Christian asks it through tears.
And perhaps the reason this question refuses to disappear is because somewhere deep inside us, we know two things simultaneously.
How can a God who is infinitely loving also be a God who judges?
How can heaven be real if hell is real too?
How can mercy and wrath exist in the same God?
To answer these questions honestly, we must resist the temptation to create a god in our own image.
Instead, we must meet the God revealed in Scripture.
And what we discover may surprise us.
Not because God is less loving than we imagined.
But because He is far more loving—and far more holy—than we ever realized.
Most people begin with the wrong assumption.
They imagine humanity as fundamentally good people occasionally making mistakes.
If that assumption were true, hell would indeed seem monstrous.
But Scripture presents a different diagnosis.
The Hebrew word often used for sin is חטא (chata').
It literally means "to miss the mark."
The Greek word used here is ἥμαρτον (hēmarton).
Again, the idea is missing the target.
The Bible's message is not that a few bad people need fixing.
It is that all people have rebelled against the God who created them.
This is where modern culture often parts ways with Scripture.
We tend to compare ourselves with other sinners.
God compares us with His holiness.
And suddenly the gap becomes infinite.
The God Nobody Wants Until Evil Touches Them
Something fascinating happens whenever evil becomes personal.
People who reject divine judgment often demand it the moment injustice affects them.
Because we instinctively know evil deserves accountability.
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh) means holy, set apart, utterly pure.
God is not merely more moral than us.
The prophet Isaiah encountered God's holiness and did not respond with self-confidence.
Because genuine encounters with God's holiness expose the truth about ourselves.
"How could a holy God allow evil to go unjudged forever?"
Jesus Talked About Hell More Than Anyone
Many assume hell was invented by angry preachers.
But the strongest warnings came from Jesus Himself.
The same Jesus who healed lepers.
The same Jesus who welcomed children.
The same Jesus who forgave sinners.
The same Jesus who willingly died on a cross.
The Greek term often used is γέεννα (Gehenna).
The name comes from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, associated with judgment and destruction.
Jesus used it as a vivid warning regarding eternal separation from God.
Love does not remain silent when danger approaches.
A doctor who discovers cancer and says nothing is not loving.
A lifeguard who sees someone drowning and remains quiet is not compassionate.
Jesus spoke about hell because He loved people enough to tell them the truth.
The Most Misunderstood Truth About Hell
Many people imagine God standing at heaven's gate looking for reasons to exclude people.
From Genesis to Revelation, the story is one of rescue.
The Greek word for perish here is ἀπόληται (apolētai).
God does not delight in judgment.
"I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked." (Ezekiel 33:11)
The Judge Himself pays the price.
If God were only holy, there would be no hope.
If God were only loving, justice would never be satisfied.
The cross is where both meet perfectly.
At Calvary, God's justice was not ignored.
God did not sweep sin under the rug.
The Greek word Jesus cried from the cross in John 19:30 was:
This single word carries astonishing weight.
But by the innocent Lamb of God.
The question is no longer whether God loves sinners.
What will we do with the love He offers?
Does God Send People to Hell?
Scripture teaches that God judges sin.
But Scripture also teaches that humanity willingly rejects Him.
C.S. Lewis famously summarized the biblical idea this way:
There are those who say to God, "Your will be done."
And there are those to whom God says, "Your will be done."
Hell is ultimately separation from God.
The tragic end of persistent rejection.
Not because God failed to love.
Not because Christ failed to save.
The doors of mercy stand open throughout this life.
The tragedy is that many walk away from them.
"Why would a loving God send anyone to hell?"
They are actually asking something deeper.
"Could God really love someone like me?"
Because beneath intellectual objections often lies personal fear.
Fear that we've gone too far.
Fear that forgiveness is for everyone except us.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The cross was not built for perfect people.
Jesus did not die for those who deserved mercy.
He died for those who desperately needed it.
Which means nobody is beyond hope while breath remains in their lungs.
Not the person reading these words right now.
The greatest evidence that God is loving is not that hell does not exist.
The greatest evidence that God is loving is that despite hell existing, He made a way for sinners to escape it.
These are not the actions of a God eager to condemn.
They are the actions of a God determined to save.
The Gospel is not the story of humanity reaching up to God.
It is the story of God reaching down to humanity.
Maybe this question has followed you for years.
Maybe you've wrestled with it in silence.
Faith is not threatened by honest questions.
But eventually every question leads to a crossroads.
Not merely what we believe about hell.
But what we believe about Jesus.
Because Christianity ultimately rises or falls on one person.
The One who stepped into our place.
The One who carried our judgment.
There may come a day when you need to read it again.
What part hit you the hardest?
One day every question will finally be answered, but the greatest tragedy would be knowing the answer and still refusing the Savior.
